items.title: One transaction per action, and a stored progress number
items.body:
**Transactions.** Starting an onboarding case writes many rows: new tasks, a status change, an activity row and an audit event. A database transaction makes them one unit: either every write commits or none does. In Prisma that is `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...)`, and every write inside must use `tx`, not the global `prisma` client, or it escapes the unit. The guide also says network calls (like sending email) do not belong inside a transaction.

**Derived data.** A case's progress could be computed on every read, or computed on write and stored in a `progressPercent` column so dashboards can sort quickly. HRFlow stores it. The price is drift: if some code path changes a task without recalculating, the stored number goes stale. So when you read the task service, check whether each path calls `recalculateOnboardingProgress` and whether it passes a `tx`.

excerpts.quote: The audit trail must be tamper-proof and written in the same transaction block as the business database updates.

* **Materialized Cache**: Calculate the value on write operations and store it in a dedicated column. * *Advantage*: Reads are extremely fast, as the database simply reads a static integer value. * *Disadvantage*: Risk of synchronization drift if updates bypass the calculation hooks.
3. **Mismatched Client Scopes**: Using the main Prisma connection object `prisma` instead of the scoped transaction argument `tx` inside callbacks.

items.title: Start here: HRFlow onboarding and the four pages this pack uses
items.body:
This repo is HRFlow, an employee-onboarding platform: an Express + Prisma backend (SQLite here) and a React frontend. HR staff create an onboarding case, start it, and the backend generates tasks from a workflow template. The `docsclaude/` folder is an 8-week course; this pack uses four of its pages. Read them in this order:

1. `03-server-mastery/05-auth-and-multi-tenancy.md` - who may do what: the permission matrix, IDOR, token lifetimes.
2. `04-architecture-and-patterns/03-transactions-and-audit.md` - why starting a case is one database transaction, and what must stay outside it.
3. `04-architecture-and-patterns/04-derived-data-and-caching.md` - the stored `progressPercent` column and how it is kept in sync.
4. `CRITIQUE.md` - an honest list of weak spots (SQLite, the Redis fallback, no retries, no token revocation).

Important habit for this pack: the guides sometimes describe the ideal ("Illustrative - not from the repo"), and several quizzes ask what the real code does. Always open the cited file under `backend/src/` and check.

items.title: When requirePermission reads the matrix
items.body:
Look at where the lookup sits. `requirePermission` runs `PermissionMatrix[permission]` in its own body and passes the resulting array to `requireRole`. `requireRole` returns a new middleware function that remembers (closes over) that array. Route files call `requirePermission('CREATE_ONBOARDING_CASE')` while the router is being built, so the lookup happens once, at route registration. Each request then runs only the returned function, which checks `allowedRoles.includes(...)`.

Why the others are wrong:
- The permission string is not compared with the role; it is a key into the matrix.
- The lookup is not inside the returned middleware, so it does not repeat on every request.
- There is no per-user cache and no lazy first-request step in this code.

excerpts.quote: export const requirePermission = (permission: keyof typeof PermissionMatrix): RequestHandler => { const allowedRoles = PermissionMatrix[permission]; return requireRole(allowedRoles); };
`requirePermission` resolves that list **once, at route-registration time** — note it runs outside the returned handler.

items.title: A reopened COMPLETED case bypasses the state machine
items.body:
In the recalculation, progress below 100 goes to the `else` branch. There, if the case's current status is `'COMPLETED'`, the code sets `data.status = 'IN_PROGRESS'` and then writes the case directly with `tx.onboardingCase.update`. It never calls the state machine, and it never sets `completedAt` to null (a comment says not to "blindly null completedAt"). So the case becomes IN_PROGRESS at 80% and keeps its old `completedAt`, even though `allowedCaseTransitions` lists `COMPLETED: []`.

Why the others are wrong:
- No `validateCaseTransition` call exists in this function, so nothing throws.
- The service does not reset `completedAt`; the comment says the opposite.
- The case does not stay COMPLETED; line 47 changes its status.

excerpts.quote: // Senior Lesson: if a completed case is reopened, do not blindly null completedAt unless requested. // We will keep status as IN_PROGRESS if progress < 100% and it was COMPLETED previously. if (currentCase.status === 'COMPLETED') { data.status = 'IN_PROGRESS'; }
PENDING_APPROVAL: ['IN_PROGRESS', 'COMPLETED', 'CANCELLED'], COMPLETED: [],

items.title: Permissions, not roles, and the IDOR trap
items.body:
Two different questions protect an API.

**Authorization by permission.** Routes do not check "is this user an HR_ADMIN?". They ask for a named permission, such as `VIEW_REPORTS`, and a single object called `PermissionMatrix` lists which roles hold each permission. `requireRole(allowedRoles)` returns the Express middleware that rejects a missing user with 401 and a wrong role with 403. `requirePermission` is a small wrapper around it. Read both functions in `requirePermission.middleware.ts` and notice which lines run when the route is defined and which run on each request.

**IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference).** Being signed in is not the same as being allowed to see a record. If a route fetches a case by the id in the URL and nothing else, any signed-in user can change the id and read someone else's case. The guide's fix is to add the user's `departmentId` (taken from the verified token, never from the request body) to the query. The guide labels its snippets "Illustrative", so check the real routers yourself.

excerpts.quote: Our platform utilizes an explicit permission-role matrix. Instead of checking a user's role directly inside routers, we check for specific **Permissions** required to execute actions.
An **IDOR** exploit occurs when an authenticated user modifies a database key (like a case ID UUID) inside a request URL to read or modify a resource belonging to another tenant or department

> **Senior aside:** *Never trust the client payload for identity context. Always resolve parameters like `departmentId` or `userId` directly from verified session tokens generated inside security middleware.*

items.title: What many simultaneous starts do to SQLite
items.body:
The critique explains that SQLite "supports only a single concurrent writer" because it locks the whole database for writing. Starting a case is one transaction with many writes, so it holds that lock for a while. When several HR managers start workflows at once, the other writers wait, and the critique predicts they "stall and throw `SQLITE_BUSY` transaction timeout errors". Critique item 3 adds that there is no retry logic, so that error reaches the user.

Why the others are wrong:
- The start path does use a transaction (`prisma.$transaction`), and the lock makes writers wait rather than silently overwrite.
- Id generation is not the problem the critique names.
- Dirty reads (seeing uncommitted data) are not what SQLite's single-writer lock produces; the critique predicts waiting and timeouts.

excerpts.quote: * **The Scaling Limit**: While SQLite is extremely fast for read operations, it supports only a single concurrent writer due to its database-level write locking mechanism. Under high concurrent write traffic (such as multiple HR managers starting workflows simultaneously), requests will stall and throw `SQLITE_BUSY` transaction timeout errors.

items.title: What really protects GET /cases/:id
items.body:
The guide's department-scoped query is marked "Illustrative - not from the repo". The real router calls `router.use(authMiddleware)` once, so every route needs a signed-in user. But the `'/:id'` route adds nothing else: no `requirePermission`, no validation, just the controller. So any authenticated user can request any case id. That is the IDOR shape the guide warns about.

Why the others are wrong:
- `authMiddleware` puts the user (with their `departmentId`) on the request, but the service's `getById` queries `where: { id }` only; no department filter is appended.
- `validate(createOnboardingCaseSchema)` is used on `POST '/'`, not on the GET by id.
- `requirePermission('VIEW_ALL_CASES')` is not on this route; the router never uses that permission.

items.title: The one-line change that lets HR specialists read audit logs
items.body:
The matrix maps each permission to the roles allowed to use it. `VIEW_AUDIT_LOGS` currently lists SYSTEM_ADMIN and HR_ADMIN. Routes ask for the permission, not for roles, so adding `Roles.HR_SPECIALIST` to that one array is enough; no route has to change. The guide says exactly this: "Adding a role to a permission is a one-line matrix edit; no route changes."

Why the others are wrong:
- Switching routes to `requireRole` with a role list is the role-hardcoding the design avoids, and touches every route.
- Making HR specialists SYSTEM_ADMIN gives them far more than audit logs; and the matrix arrays can take any role.
- A role check inside the controller is pitfall 2 in the guide's checklist ("Role Hardcoding inside Controllers").

excerpts.quote: VIEW_AUDIT_LOGS: [Roles.SYSTEM_ADMIN, Roles.HR_ADMIN],
Adding a role to a permission is a one-line matrix edit; no route changes.
2. **Role Hardcoding inside Controllers**: Writing `if (user.role === 'HR_ADMIN')` inside service files instead of using permission-based middleware check gates.

items.title: Why a failed audit write leaves the database unchanged
items.body:
`startOnboardingCase` wraps all its work in `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...)`, and every write inside uses `tx`: the task creates, the case update to IN_PROGRESS, the activity row, and finally `tx.auditEvent.create`. If that last write throws, the transaction aborts and the database rolls back everything done inside it. The guide: the whole transaction "is rolled back instantly". Either the action and its audit both exist, or neither does.

Why the others are wrong:
- Tasks and status cannot persist alone; they were written through the same `tx`.
- There is no notification-queue retry for audits; the notification is sent by the controller after the transaction, not inside it.
- Tasks are created before the audit write (in the loop above it), and they roll back too.

excerpts.quote: return prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
await tx.auditEvent.create({
If the database fails to write the `auditEvent` record, the entire transaction (including case status updates and concrete task generations) is rolled back instantly.

items.title: Why the in-memory email fallback loses mail on restart
items.body:
`createAndProcessEmail` first writes the email row with `status: 'PENDING'`. If Redis is not connected, it does not queue anything durable: it calls `setTimeout(..., 500)` to run `deliverEmailMock` half a second later. That timer exists only in the memory of the running Node process. If the process restarts after 200 ms, the timer is gone, delivery never runs, and the row stays PENDING. The critique: "all pending notifications are lost forever".

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing is sent synchronously; the send is inside the delayed callback.
- No startup code re-queues PENDING rows; the only later write to the email row is in the delivery function itself.
- BullMQ never saw this job: `notificationsQueue.add` runs only when Redis is connected.

excerpts.quote: if (isRedisConnected && notificationsQueue) { await notificationsQueue.add('sendEmail', { emailId: emailRecord.id }); } else { // In-Memory Fallback: run in a non-blocking background Promise setTimeout(async () => { try { await this.deliverEmailMock(emailRecord.id);
all pending notifications are lost forever. There is zero durability or retry persistence.

items.title: Why a stolen access token outlives logout
items.body:
An access token is a signed JWT. `verifyAccessToken` only calls `jwt.verify` with the access secret: if the signature is good and the token has not expired, it passes. Nothing on the server remembers that the user logged out. The critique says so directly: there is no blacklist, so the token "remains cryptographically valid until its expiration window passes". The window is `JWT_ACCESS_EXPIRES_IN`, which defaults to `'15m'`.

Why the others are wrong:
- Logout does not delete the access token server-side; the critique says the frontend only clears its own store.
- 7 days (`'7d'`) is the refresh token's default lifetime, not the access token's.
- Logging in again does not change `JWT_ACCESS_SECRET`; it is a fixed config value read from the environment.

excerpts.quote: export const verifyAccessToken = (token: string): JwtPayload => { return jwt.verify(token, env.JWT_ACCESS_SECRET) as JwtPayload; };
JWT_ACCESS_EXPIRES_IN: z.string().default('15m'), JWT_REFRESH_EXPIRES_IN: z.string().default('7d'),
the access token remains cryptographically valid until its expiration window passes

items.title: The direct task-status path is not one transaction
items.body:
The derived-data guide claims every status update recalculates "inside the same transaction block". Read the direct path at the end of the task service's update method. It calls `prisma.onboardingTask.update`, then `prisma.onboardingActivity.create`, then `recalculateOnboardingProgress(task.onboardingCaseId)`. All three use the base `prisma` client, and the recalculation is called with no `tx` argument. They are separate calls, so if a later one fails the earlier ones stay, and the stored progress can drift. (The approval branch earlier in the method does use `prisma.$transaction`.)

Why the others are wrong:
- The recalculation runs after the task update (line 240 comes after line 198), not before.
- It does recalculate on this path, guarded by `isProgressAffected`.
- No `prisma.$transaction` wraps these calls, so the guide's sentence is too strong for this path.

excerpts.quote: const updatedTask = await prisma.onboardingTask.update({
if (isProgressAffected) { await OnboardingProgressService.recalculateOnboardingProgress(task.onboardingCaseId); }
triggers `recalculateOnboardingProgress` inside the same transaction block

items.title: Why the start notification is sent after the transaction
items.body:
The controller first awaits `OnboardingCasesService.startOnboardingCase`, which only resolves after its transaction commits. Only then does it import the notification service and call `sendOnboardingStarted`, inside its own `try`/`catch` that just logs a warning. This follows the guide's rule: "Never execute external network calls inside a transaction block". It also means a failed send cannot undo a start that already committed.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing in the guide or code says Prisma forbids dynamic `import()` inside a transaction callback.
- The call passes only `result.case.id`; it uses no audit event id and no second transaction.
- An email sent after commit cannot roll anything back, and the controller does not wait on the email to decide whether the start stands.

excerpts.quote: const result = await OnboardingCasesService.startOnboardingCase(req.params.id, actorId); // Queue WELCOME email notifications after successful transaction try { const { NotificationService } = await import('../notifications/notification.service'); const email = result.case.employeeProfileId; // Or fetch email profile await NotificationService.sendOnboardingStarted(result.case.id); } catch (err) { console.warn('⚠️ Background notification enqueuing failed post-transaction:', err); }
Never execute external network calls inside a transaction block, as external latency can tie up database connections and crash the pool.

items.title: What MANAGER can do according to PermissionMatrix
items.body:
Read the matrix line by line and look for `Roles.MANAGER`. It appears in exactly one entry: `APPROVE_MANAGER_STEP`, where it sits next to `SYSTEM_ADMIN`. Managers approve their step in the workflow; nothing else in the matrix lists them.

Why the others are wrong:
- `VIEW_ALL_CASES` lists SYSTEM_ADMIN, HR_ADMIN and HR_SPECIALIST, not MANAGER.
- `COMPLETE_IT_TASK` is held by SYSTEM_ADMIN and IT_ADMIN only.
- `VIEW_REPORTS` is for SYSTEM_ADMIN, HR_ADMIN and HR_SPECIALIST, so MANAGER does not hold it alongside the approval permission.

excerpts.quote: VIEW_ALL_CASES: [Roles.SYSTEM_ADMIN, Roles.HR_ADMIN, Roles.HR_SPECIALIST],
VIEW_REPORTS: [Roles.SYSTEM_ADMIN, Roles.HR_ADMIN, Roles.HR_SPECIALIST],
APPROVE_MANAGER_STEP: [Roles.SYSTEM_ADMIN, Roles.MANAGER], COMPLETE_IT_TASK: [Roles.SYSTEM_ADMIN, Roles.IT_ADMIN],

items.title: Why 2 completed and 1 skipped out of 6 tasks gives 50
items.body:
`recalculateOnboardingProgress` loads every task of the case, then counts a task as done if its status is `'COMPLETED'` **or** `'SKIPPED'`. Here that is 2 + 1 = 3 tasks out of 6. The stored value is `Math.round((3 / 6) * 100)` = 50. The TODO and PENDING_APPROVAL tasks are not done, so they count only in the total.

Why the others are wrong:
- 67 would be 4 of 6, which would need PENDING_APPROVAL to count as done; the filter does not list it.
- 33 is 2 of 6: it forgets that SKIPPED counts as done.
- 83 is 5 of 6, counting everything except one task.

excerpts.quote: const completed = tasks.filter( (task: any) => task.status === 'COMPLETED' || task.status === 'SKIPPED' ).length; const progress = Math.round((completed / total) * 100);
